fieldNotes.title: Field Notes: The 3.4 Buy Buttons Per Checkout
fieldNotes.source: Anonymous product designer at MetroBites, a Chennai-based quick-commerce food delivery app
fieldNotes.story:
MetroBites had a payment-confirmation problem nobody had a name for. The technical metric the engineering team watched was *retry rate*: how often a single user tapped the **Pay ₹** button more than once on the same order. The number, in late 2024, was **3.4 taps on average**. Some users tapped seven times. The payment infra was billed per attempted transaction; this alone cost the company **₹14 lakh a month** in extra gateway fees, before counting the support load.

The root cause was a 3.2-second delay between tap and any visible response. The screen sat there. No spinner. No state change on the button. No copy. Users — entirely reasonably — assumed the tap hadn't registered, and tapped again. And again. Then a third time, this time *harder*, as if the screen could feel desperation.

The redesign shipped on **January 22, 2025**: an optimistic UI pattern where the button immediately changed to a disabled state with a spinner and the copy *"Confirming with your bank..."*, paired with a small line below — *"This usually takes 2-4 seconds."* The actual confirmation latency did not change. The interaction redesign took a senior designer four hours including the copy reviews.

Retries dropped **73%** in the first two weeks. Gateway fees fell by **₹10.2 lakh in February**. Customer support tickets tagged *"payment failed but money debited"* dropped from 312 to 41 a week. The CFO mentioned it on the next earnings call, attributed it to *"engineering improvements."*
fieldNotes.takeaway: If your interface goes silent during the hardest 3 seconds of a user's day, they will not assume it is working.

bossBattle.title: Vikram's Payment Confirmation
bossBattle.setup:
Eight weeks into the **Saral Pay** engagement. Vikram is wiring up the new Send Money flow and hits the same wall every fintech hits: the bank's confirmation API takes between **1.8 and 4.5 seconds** to respond. He pings you: *"What do I show during that gap? Engineering wants to know if a spinner is enough."*

You know it isn't.

coach.name: Design-Director Diya
coach.role: Once made a deck called 'Loading States Are a Design Problem, Not an Engineering One.' Has shown it 47 times.

stages.prompt: Vikram's first proposal: **"Just put a spinner in the middle of the screen and grey out the button. Standard pattern."** What do you push back with?

options.label: "A spinner alone is decoration. The user needs three things: confirmation that the tap registered, a sense of *what* is happening, and a sense of *how long*. A spinner gives one of three."
options.explain: **Yes.** You named the user's three latent questions. *Did it register? What's happening? How long?* Every loading state worth shipping answers all three.

options.label: "Spinners are fine for short waits. But 4.5 seconds is long, so use a progress bar instead."
options.explain: Progress bar implies determinism. Bank APIs are non-deterministic — sometimes 1.8s, sometimes 4.5s. Your bar will sit at 80% for 3 seconds and users will think it's stuck. You traded one bad signal for another.

options.label: "Sure, ship it."
options.explain: MetroBites's CFO is currently writing your eulogy. Vikram ships, retries spike, gateway costs balloon, and three weeks from now he asks you why payment volume is fine but margin is shrinking.

options.label: "Add a fun animation — keep users entertained while they wait."
options.explain: Users are not bored, they are *anxious about whether they just sent ₹50,000 to the wrong UPI ID.* A dancing rupee symbol is condescending. Diya is making the *no* hand gesture from across the room.

stages.prompt: You convince Vikram. Now: **what does the button itself do** the moment the user taps?

options.label: Button instantly changes to a disabled state with an inline spinner *and* the copy `Confirming...`. Stays in place — does not jump.
options.explain: **This is the move.** Optimistic UI: act immediately, narrate quietly, don't move the screen around. The user gets feedback inside the 100ms window the brain treats as *cause and effect*.

options.label: Button disappears; a full-screen modal slides up with `Processing your payment`.
options.explain: You broke the spatial relationship between cause (tap) and effect (response). Users now wonder if the button broke. Modals are also expensive to dismiss if something goes wrong — you're now two screens deep in an error.

options.label: Button stays the same; a small spinner appears next to it.
options.explain: If the button still looks tappable, users will tap again to be sure. You spent two stages avoiding this exact failure and re-enabled it.

options.label: Button becomes a circular progress indicator that fills clockwise.
options.explain: Same problem as the progress bar — implies determinism you don't have. Also: the circular fill takes longer than 4.5 seconds visually if you make it smooth, so users see it *finish* before the API responds. Now they're confused *and* frustrated.

stages.prompt: The button is handled. Vikram asks: **"What about the copy? Engineering said `Loading...` is fine."** What microcopy do you ship?

options.label: **`Confirming with your bank... usually 2 to 4 seconds`** — names *who* is doing the work, sets a *time expectation*, no full stop.
options.explain: **Strong.** *Confirming with your bank* externalises the wait — it's the bank's slowness, not yours. *2 to 4 seconds* sets a rough expectation without overpromising. Users will tolerate twice the wait if you tell them the wait exists.

options.label: **`Loading...`** — minimal, doesn't make promises.
options.explain: *Loading* is a developer word, not a human word. It also tells the user nothing they don't already know from the spinner. You used three letters of screen real estate to add zero information.

options.label: **`Please wait while we process your transaction. Do not refresh or close this page.`** — explicit and safe.
options.explain: Banking-portal energy from 2007. Long, defensive, unfriendly, and the *do not close* warning *creates* the anxiety it's trying to prevent. Users will now panic-tap.

options.label: **`Hold tight! ✨ We're working some magic with your bank ✨`** — friendly and warm.
options.explain: The user is sending money. They want competence, not whimsy. The sparkle emojis on a transaction screen will make a 45-year-old uncle close the app and call you. Diya has stopped responding to your pings.

stages.prompt: Vikram asks the final question: **"What if the bank takes more than 4 seconds? Or fails?"** This is the failure-mode microcopy. What do you ship?

options.label: At 5s, copy switches to `Taking longer than usual — we will not double-charge you.` On hard failure: `Payment did not go through. No money was deducted. Try again or use a different method.`
options.explain: **Lands it.** The 5-second copy preempts the *exact* fear that drives multi-tap ("will I be charged twice?"). The failure copy names the consequence (`No money was deducted`) before offering the action. Both written in human language.

options.label: At 5s, show a spinner forever and hope it resolves.
options.explain: Users will close the app, reopen it, and find their money in limbo. Support tickets will spike. You're back to MetroBites's ₹14 lakh problem, just with a nicer button.

options.label: On failure: `Error 500: Payment gateway timeout. Please try again later.`
options.explain: Engineer copy. Users do not know what 500 means and do not care. They want to know: *is my money gone?* Tell them that or you've failed at the only thing the screen had to do.

options.label: Add a `Cancel` link below the spinner that the user can tap if they get worried.
options.explain: **Smart secondary.** Even if cancel doesn't actually stop the API call (it can't, after a certain point), the *option to escape* dramatically reduces anxiety. Pair this with the 5-second copy switch and you've covered both axes.

outcomes.perfect: Saral Pay's new Send Money ships in week 9. Vikram emails the team after the first week of data: *"Retries down 68%, support tickets for 'didn't go through' down 80%."* You quietly celebrate. **Diya sends one word: 'good.'**
outcomes.good: You got the optimistic UI right but one of the copy lines is doing too much (or too little) work. Real users will mostly forgive you. Re-read the section on **how microcopy answers the user's actual fears**, not the developer's mental model.
outcomes.learn: Either users still feel the wait (because the button looks unchanged) or the copy made things worse. Re-read the lesson — especially the section on **the three latent questions** every loading state must answer in under 4 seconds.
